about.paragraph_1: The Canadian Digit Triplet Test (CDTT) is a hearing screening tool developed by a team of researchers at the University of Ottawa and the University of Toronto. The test uses an adaptive procedure to determine the speech recognition threshold (SRT) for digit triplets in noise. The CDTT follows the guidelines of the International Collegium of Rehabilitative Audiology (<icraLink>ICRA</icraLink>) for the construction of <multilangualSpeechLink>multilingual speech tests</multilangualSpeechLink>.
about.link_2_title: Test development article in JASA Express Letters

paragraph_2.before_link_1: The CDTT was first made available for testing in the two official languages of Canada, English and French, using digits from a bilingual male and a bilingual female presented in speech-spectrum noise. The test has been included in two large-scale multi-site national studies, the
paragraph_2.link_1_title: Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging
paragraph_2.after_link_2: , and made available to other researchers. Additional language modules have been developed in Asante-Twi and Ghanaian English.

about.bullet_pts_1: The <goToLink>research software platform</goToLink> is the most comprehensive version of the CDTT. It provides complete control over the test parameters and allows for the easy integration of new language/talker modules and additional user-defined noise maskers. Researchers can apply for a non-commercial software license for academic and research purposes.
about.bullet_pts_2: An <goToLink>online version</goToLink> is available for demonstration purposes.

section_1.title: Software and hardware considerations
section_1.paragraph_1: The CDTT software was developed as a cross-platform Java application and it can be run on different operating systems (e.g., Windows, macOS).

bullet_pts.1: The main interface provides controls for the test operator to enter participant information, select test parameters, run a test, and save the results in MS-Excel.
bullet_pts.2: Participants enter their digit responses on-screen or using an external USB numeric keypad.
bullet_pts.3: Use of an external USB sound card (e.g., E10K Olympus 2 by FiiO) is recommend for portability and reproducibility across computers.
bullet_pts.4: Results have been found to be largely insensitive to the choice of earphones, but use of Radioear DD45 audiometric earphones is recommended for strict comparison to the
bullet_pts.5: Results obtained to date suggest that hearing screening with the CDTT can be administered with supra-aural earphones (Radioear DD45 or similar) on testing sites with background noise levels not exceeding 60 dBA, while the use of sound-attenuating circumaural earphones (Radioear DD450 or similar) should be considered on testing sites with background noise levels up to 75 dBA.

bullet_pts.1: Testing languages: Canadian English and French (2016), Asante-Twi and Ghanaian English (2023)
bullet_pts.2: Talkers: one or two talkers (male and female) per language/dialect
bullet_pts.4: Maskers: Talker-specific speech spectrum noise (default) and user-defined noises
bullet_pts.5: Test modes: Adaptative speech-recognition threshold search (SRT) or fixed signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)
